```{r}
) |> dplyr::mutate(term = factor(term, levels = term_levels))

# Full effect-size sweep, all points (not just the own-effect-size slice) --
# used for the Aim 1 power-curves figure below.
aim1_sweep_combined <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  aim1_hlva        |> dplyr::filter(term == "zHLVA"),
  aim1_pcref       |> dplyr::filter(term == "zPCREFp"),
  aim1_interaction |> dplyr::filter(term == "zHLVA:zPCREFp")
) |> dplyr::mutate(term = factor(term, levels = term_levels))

# Shared summary helper: power, sign reliability, Type S error rate,
# Type M ratio, median bias, and coverage, grouped by whatever columns are
# passed in `group_vars`.
summarize_p2_metrics <- function(df, group_vars) {
  df |>
    dplyr::group_by(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(group_vars))) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      power            = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE),
      sign_reliability = mean(correct_sign, na.rm = TRUE),
      type_s_rate      = mean(sign_error[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),
      type_m_ratio     = median(inflation_ratio[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),
      median_bias      = median(bias, na.rm = TRUE),
      coverage         = mean(covers_truth, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_fits           = dplyr::n(),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

aim1_metric_labels <- c(power = "Power\nP(significant)",
                         sign_reliability = "Sign reliability\nP(correct sign)",
                         type_s_rate = "Type S rate\nP(wrong sign | significant)",
                         type_m_ratio = "Type M ratio\nmedian |est/true| | significant")

aim2_metric_labels <- c(discovery_rate = "Discovery rate\nP(significant, half 1)",
                         replication_rate = "Replication rate\nP(sig. + same sign, both halves)",
                         conditional_replication = "Conditional replication\nP(replicates | discovery-sig.)")
```

## Shared plotting helpers

Aim 1 and Aim 2 each need a metrics-vs-`n_t` line/facet plot and an
`n_p`x`n_t` heatmap that differ only in which columns/labels are used. Both
are written once here and reused for each aim below (and are intended to be
reused again for the Aims 3-6 documents still to come).

```{r}
#| label: plot-helpers

plot_metrics_vs_x <- function(data, x_var, metrics, metric_labels,
                               color_var = "term", x_lab = NULL, x_breaks = n_t_grid) {
  x_lab <- x_lab %||% x_var
  df_long <- data |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::all_of(metrics), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
    dplyr::mutate(metric = factor(metric_labels[metric], levels = unname(metric_labels)))

  ggplot(df_long, aes(x = .data[[x_var]], y = value, color = .data[[color_var]])) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = x_breaks) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
    labs(x = x_lab, y = NULL, color = "Term") +
    theme_minimal()
}

plot_power_heatmap <- function(data, fill_var, facet_var = "term", fill_label = "Value",
                                grid_n_p = n_p_grid, grid_n_t = n_t_grid,
                                limits = c(0, 1), label_format = c("percent", "number"),
                                digits = 2, diverging = FALSE, midpoint = 0, squish = FALSE) {
  # Generalized from a power-only heatmap to any (n_p, n_t) diagnostic
  # surface. Defaults (limits = c(0, 1), percent labels, no squishing)
  # exactly reproduce the original power/replication-rate behavior, so
  # existing calls below are unaffected. `label_format = "number"` and/or
  # `diverging = TRUE` support diagnostics that aren't bounded proportions
  # (Type M ratio, median bias, RMSE); `squish = TRUE` lets a handful of
  # extreme outlier cells (common at n_t = 2) recolor to the scale's edge
  # color rather than stretching the whole gradient to accommodate them --
  # the text label still shows the real, uncapped value.
  label_format <- match.arg(label_format)
  label_fn <- if (label_format == "percent") {
    function(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1)
  } else {
    function(x) sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), x)
  }
  oob_fn <- if (squish) scales::squish else scales::censor

  p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = factor(n_p, levels = grid_n_p), y = factor(n_t, levels = grid_n_t),
                    fill = .data[[fill_var]])) +
    geom_tile() +
    geom_text(aes(label = label_fn(.data[[fill_var]])), size = 2.8,
              color = if (diverging) "black" else "white") +
    facet_wrap(stats::as.formula(paste0("~", facet_var))) +
    labs(x = "Participant sample size (n_p)", y = "Text sample size (n_t)", fill = fill_label) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

  if (diverging) {
    p + scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",
                              midpoint = midpoint, limits = limits, oob = oob_fn)
  } else if (label_format == "percent") {
    p + scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = limits, labels = scales::percent, oob = oob_fn)
  } else {
    p + scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = limits, oob = oob_fn)
  }
}
```

## Aim 1: is small-text-*N* instability a text-margin property or an interaction-specific property?

At each effect's own empirically-observed value, sign reliability and power
by `n_t`:

| `n_t` | zHLVA sign reliability | zPCREFp sign reliability | interaction sign reliability | zHLVA power | zPCREFp power | interaction power |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0.940 | **0.553** | 0.717 | 0.650 | 0.627 | 0.127 |
| 10 | 0.997 | 0.730 | 0.920 | 0.897 | 0.177 | 0.603 |
| 35 | 0.997 | 0.860 | 0.930 | 0.917 | 0.300 | 0.577 |
| 85 | 0.993 | 0.930 | 0.897 | 0.920 | 0.420 | 0.570 |
| 136 | 0.993 | 0.937 | 0.913 | 0.910 | 0.510 | 0.620 |

**This resolves the question the design set out to answer, and the answer is
not what the "reverse cohesion effect" framing might suggest.** At `n_t =
2`, `zPCREFp`'s sign reliability (0.553) is *worse* than the interaction's
(0.717) -- barely better than a coin flip -- while `zHLVA` (the
participant-level effect) is comparatively well-behaved (0.940). This is a
**text-margin property, not an interaction-specific property**: the
text-level main effect is at least as unstable as the interaction at the
smallest realistic text sample size, and by this particular diagnostic, more
so.

`zPCREFp`'s power also shows the "underpowered paradox" signature directly:
power is *higher* at `n_t = 2` (0.627) than at `n_t = 10` (0.177) -- not
because small samples are better powered, but because the noisiest, most
degenerate cell produces wildly inflated estimates that cross the
significance threshold more often *while being wrong about the sign* half
the time. A researcher who only sees "significant, p < .05" from a 2-text
study cannot distinguish this from a well-powered result.

### Aim 1 -- fuller metrics table

The table above reports sign reliability and power only. For completeness
against Marek et al.'s (2022) full diagnostic set, this expands to
**Type I (false-positive) rate**, Type S error rate, Type M ratio, median
bias, coverage, and RMSE. All columns except the new Type I column are
computed at each term's own empirically-observed effect size, pooled across
the six participant sample sizes; the Type I column instead comes from the
`effect_value = 0` point on the same sweep (the true-null case), since a
false-positive rate is only defined when there is nothing true to detect.
Surfacing it as an explicit table column (rather than leaving it visible
only as the orange curve in Figure 4, further below) makes it directly
comparable, row by row, against power and the other error rates.

```{r}
#| label: aim1-full-metrics-table

aim1_metrics_by_nt <- aim1_all |>
  dplyr::group_by(term, n_t) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    power            = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE),
    sign_reliability = mean(correct_sign, na.rm = TRUE),
    type_s_rate      = mean(sign_error[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),
    type_m_ratio     = median(inflation_ratio[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),
    median_bias      = median(bias, na.rm = TRUE),
    coverage         = mean(covers_truth, na.rm = TRUE),
    rmse_raw         = sqrt(mean(bias^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
    rmse_trimmed     = sqrt(mean(pmin(bias^2, quantile(bias^2, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)), na.rm = TRUE)),
    n_fits           = dplyr::n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

aim1_type1_by_nt <- aim1_sweep_combined |>
  dplyr::filter(effect_value == 0) |>
  dplyr::group_by(term, n_t) |>
  dplyr::summarise(type_1_rate = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

aim1_metrics_by_nt <- aim1_metrics_by_nt |>
  dplyr::left_join(aim1_type1_by_nt, by = c("term", "n_t")) |>
  dplyr::relocate(type_1_rate, .after = power)

aim1_metrics_by_nt |>
  dplyr::arrange(term, n_t) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Term", "n_t", "Power", "Type I rate", "Sign reliability",
                  "Type S rate", "Type M ratio", "Median bias", "Coverage",
                  "RMSE (raw)", "RMSE (trimmed)", "n fits")
  )
```

`rmse_raw` is included for completeness but is itself dominated by rare
pathological fits at small `n_t` (e.g. an outlying -20.3 estimate at
`n_t = 2`); `rmse_trimmed` (winsorizing squared bias at its 95th percentile
before averaging) is the more trustworthy summary of typical-case error
magnitude and should be preferred when comparing across cells. Note that
`type_1_rate` is nominally expected to be ~0.05 under correct calibration --
values well above that (as for `zPCREFp` at small `n_t`, previewed in the
summary table above and detailed mechanistically below) indicate
miscalibration, not merely bad luck.

### Aim 1 -- visualizations

#### Visualizations of power and error surfaces: showing power or error rate variation over variation in text sample size x participant sample size, for observed effects

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim1-power-surface
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Aim 1: power surface across the full joint (n_p, n_t) grid, at each term's own empirically-observed effect size. This is the direct 2-D analog of a Marek et al. (2022)-style Figure 3 sample-size surface: both axes are the two sample-size margins, and tile fill is the probability a 95% Wald CI excludes zero."

aim1_surface <- aim1_all |>
  dplyr::group_by(term, n_p, n_t) |>
  dplyr::summarise(power = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

plot_power_heatmap(aim1_surface, fill_var = "power", fill_label = "Power")
```

The surface makes visible what the by-`n_t` table (pooled over `n_p`)
cannot -- and the accurate picture is more nuanced than a coarse read
suggests (the numbers below were checked directly against
`aim1_surface`). `zHLVA` is the best-behaved term, but its saturation is
**not** independent of `n_t`: at `n_t >= 10`, power already reaches
92-100% by `n_p = 100`; at `n_t = 2`, the same `n_p = 100` cell reaches
only 46%, and power doesn't approach that ceiling (92%) until `n_p =
1300`. `n_t = 2` still measurably slows `zHLVA` down -- just far less than
it does the two text-margin terms.

`zPCREFp` and the interaction, once the full surface is examined, turn out
to diverge sharply from each other, not just from `zHLVA`. The
**interaction** genuinely needs growth on both margins: at `n_t = 2` its
power never exceeds 24% anywhere on the `n_p` grid (2-24%), while at
`n_t >= 10` it reaches 90-96% by `n_p = 1300`+ -- a real, large power gain
from a bigger text sample. **`zPCREFp` does not show this pattern.** At
matched `n_p`, its power at `n_t = 2` (20-88% across the `n_p` grid) meets
or exceeds its power at *every* larger `n_t` in the grid (10, 35, 85, and
136) in 5 of 6 `n_p` cells -- e.g. at `n_p = 1300`, `n_t = 2` reaches 88%
while the best any larger `n_t` achieves there is 72% (`n_t = 136`). This
is not `zPCREFp` being well-powered at `n_t = 2`; it is the underpowered
paradox previewed above, visible directly on the surface -- the apparent
"power" at `n_t = 2` is inflated by the same singular-fit false-positive
mechanism documented later in this section, not a sign that more
participants are working as they should for this term.

::: {.callout-important}
## A second, independent illustration of the underpowered paradox

The `n_t = 2` reversal above is worth flagging explicitly as its **own**
piece of evidence for the underpowered paradox, distinct from the sign-
reliability/Type S evidence discussed earlier (`zPCREFp`'s 0.553 sign
reliability at `n_t = 2`, worse than the interaction's) and later
(the Type S/Type M curves). That evidence all requires first conditioning
on which fits were "significant" and then asking whether their *sign* was
right. The power-surface reversal needs no such conditioning: it shows up
in the raw significance rate itself, at every single `n_p` on the grid
(not just pooled, as in the earlier by-`n_t` table), without ever
inspecting sign or magnitude. Two structurally different diagnostics --
one about whether significant results have the correct sign, one about
how often results are significant at all -- point to the same underlying
`n_t = 2` identifiability breakdown, which is stronger corroboration than
either diagnostic could provide alone.
:::

The same `(n_p, n_t)` surface can be drawn for every other diagnostic in
the fuller metrics table above, not just power -- doing so shows directly
whether the text-margin concentration visible in the power surface is a
general property of the smallest cells or specific to power itself. These
seven surfaces are computed by term x `n_p` x `n_t` (i.e. one level finer
than the by-`n_t`-only fuller metrics table above, which pools over `n_p`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim1-error-surfaces
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 16
#| fig-cap: "Aim 1: the remaining seven diagnostics from the fuller metrics table, each drawn as its own (n_p, n_t) surface (the same layout as the power surface above). Type I rate, sign reliability, Type S rate, and coverage share the fixed [0, 100%] color scale used for power, for direct comparability; Type M ratio and RMSE (trimmed) use a free color scale, capped (squished, not truncated -- the printed number is always the true value) at a fixed upper limit so that rare extreme outlier cells at n_t = 2 don't wash out the rest of the scale; median bias uses a diverging scale centered at zero."

aim1_surfaces_extra <- aim1_all |>
  dplyr::group_by(term, n_p, n_t) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    sign_reliability = mean(correct_sign, na.rm = TRUE),
    type_s_rate      = mean(sign_error[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),
    type_m_ratio     = median(inflation_ratio[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),
    median_bias      = median(bias, na.rm = TRUE),
    coverage         = mean(covers_truth, na.rm = TRUE),
    rmse_trimmed     = sqrt(mean(pmin(bias^2, quantile(bias^2, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)), na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

aim1_type1_surface <- aim1_sweep_combined |>
  dplyr::filter(effect_value == 0) |>
  dplyr::group_by(term, n_p, n_t) |>
  dplyr::summarise(type_1_rate = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

aim1_surfaces_extra <- aim1_surfaces_extra |>
  dplyr::left_join(aim1_type1_surface, by = c("term", "n_p", "n_t"))

bias_limit <- max(abs(aim1_surfaces_extra$median_bias), na.rm = TRUE)

panel_surface_type1 <- plot_power_heatmap(
  aim1_surfaces_extra, fill_var = "type_1_rate", fill_label = "Type I\nrate"
) + labs(title = "Type I (false-positive) rate")

panel_surface_signrel <- plot_power_heatmap(
  aim1_surfaces_extra, fill_var = "sign_reliability", fill_label = "Sign\nreliability"
) + labs(title = "Sign reliability")

panel_surface_types <- plot_power_heatmap(
  aim1_surfaces_extra, fill_var = "type_s_rate", fill_label = "Type S\nrate"
) + labs(title = "Type S (sign) error rate")

panel_surface_coverage <- plot_power_heatmap(
  aim1_surfaces_extra, fill_var = "coverage", fill_label = "Coverage"
) + labs(title = "95% CI coverage")

panel_surface_typem <- plot_power_heatmap(
  aim1_surfaces_extra, fill_var = "type_m_ratio", fill_label = "Type M\nratio",
  limits = c(0, 10), label_format = "number", digits = 1, squish = TRUE
) + labs(title = "Type M (magnitude) ratio")

panel_surface_bias <- plot_power_heatmap(
  aim1_surfaces_extra, fill_var = "median_bias", fill_label = "Median\nbias",
  limits = c(-bias_limit, bias_limit), label_format = "number", digits = 3, diverging = TRUE
) + labs(title = "Median bias")

panel_surface_rmse <- plot_power_heatmap(
  aim1_surfaces_extra, fill_var = "rmse_trimmed", fill_label = "RMSE\n(trimmed)",
  limits = c(0, 1.5), label_format = "number", digits = 2, squish = TRUE
) + labs(title = "RMSE (trimmed)")

patchwork::wrap_plots(
  panel_surface_type1, panel_surface_signrel, panel_surface_types, panel_surface_coverage,
  panel_surface_typem, panel_surface_bias, panel_surface_rmse,
  ncol = 2
)
```

Three findings stand out. First, **Type I rate, sign reliability, Type S
rate, and coverage all show the same qualitative pattern as power**: the
worst cells are concentrated at `n_t = 2`, and (for `zPCREFp` and the
interaction) growing `n_p` alone at `n_t = 2` does not fix them --
confirming that the text-margin concentration already established for
power is a general property of this design's smallest cells, not specific
to the power diagnostic. Coverage is the starkest illustration: nominal
coverage should be ~95% everywhere, but `zPCREFp`'s coverage at `n_t = 2`
falls to as low as 10-12% at the *largest* participant sample sizes (`n_p`
= 1300-1497) -- more data on the wrong margin makes the miscalibration
*more* confidently wrong, not less, exactly the "overconfident, too-narrow
Wald SE" mechanism documented later in this section.

Second, **the Type M ratio panel needs a specific interpretive caveat**:
its most extreme cell (the interaction, `n_p = 25`, `n_t = 2`, median ratio
~85x, squished to the scale's dark edge here) is not evidence of an
enormous absolute error -- the interaction's own effect size is only
0.054, so even a modest absolute bias becomes a huge *ratio* when divided
by a true value that small. The median bias panel alongside it shows this
directly: median bias stays within +/-0.12 in every cell on this entire
grid, including the ones with triple-digit Type M ratios. Ratio-based
inflation measures like Type M are most informative for effects of
moderate-to-large size and can be misleadingly dramatic-looking for a
near-zero true effect; this document's own `zHLVA:zPCREFp` sweep is a
concrete illustration of that general statistical caveat, not a sign of a
uniquely severe problem with the interaction term.

(A related, more mundane artifact: one cell -- the interaction at
`n_p = 100, n_t = 85` -- shows as blank/grey in the Type S and Type M
panels. Both diagnostics are conditional on significance, and this
particular cell happened to have zero significant fits among its 50
replicates; dividing by zero significant fits leaves the diagnostic
undefined rather than zero, which `ggplot2` renders as a missing tile
rather than a colored one. This is a small-sample artifact of this
specific `(n_p, n_t)` cell, not a data error.)

Third, the **RMSE (trimmed) surface differs from the by-`n_t`-only version
in the fuller metrics table above** because it is computed per `(term,
n_p, n_t)` cell here (50 replicates) rather than pooled over all six `n_p`
values (300 replicates) -- the finer grouping means the within-cell 95th-
percentile winsorization threshold is itself estimated from fewer points,
so it is less robust to a single extreme replicate (e.g. `zHLVA` at `n_p =
25, n_t = 2`, where one pathological fit still pulls the trimmed RMSE up
to 2.86 despite `zHLVA` otherwise behaving well at that cell). Treat the
by-`n_t`-only table's RMSE column as the more stable summary, and this
finer surface as showing *where* that instability is concentrated rather
than as a precise per-cell estimate in its own right.

#### Visualizations of power or error rate (sign reliability, type S, type M) variation over variation in text sample size and over participant sample size, for observed effects

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim1-metrics-vs-np
#| fig-cap: "Aim 1: power, sign reliability, Type S error rate, and Type M exaggeration ratio vs. participant sample size (n_p), at each term's own empirically-observed effect size, pooled across all five text sample sizes and 50 replicates/cell."

aim1_metrics_by_np <- aim1_all |>
  dplyr::group_by(term, n_p) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    power            = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE),
    sign_reliability = mean(correct_sign, na.rm = TRUE),
    type_s_rate      = mean(sign_error[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),
    type_m_ratio     = median(inflation_ratio[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),
    n_fits           = dplyr::n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

plot_metrics_vs_x(
  aim1_metrics_by_np, x_var = "n_p",
  metrics = c("power", "sign_reliability", "type_s_rate", "type_m_ratio"),
  metric_labels = aim1_metric_labels,
  x_lab = "Participant sample size (n_p, log scale)",
  x_breaks = n_p_grid
)
```

This is the participant-margin counterpart of the text-margin figure
below: the same four diagnostics, pooled over all five `n_t` values
instead of all six `n_p` values, so the two figures together examine each
diagnostic over both margins. `zHLVA`'s curves here should look like
conventional, well-behaved diagnostics improving monotonically with `n_p`
(power and sign reliability rising, Type S/M falling), consistent with it
being the participant-margin-limited effect; `zPCREFp` and the interaction
are pooled here across text sample sizes that range from the pathological
`n_t = 2` up to the well-behaved `n_t = 136`, so any distinctive `n_t = 2`
signature (the underpowered paradox) is diluted rather than isolated in
this view -- the `n_t`-axis figure below, and the full `(n_p, n_t)`
surfaces above, remain the more direct way to see that pathology.

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim1-metrics-vs-nt
#| fig-cap: "Aim 1: power, sign reliability, Type S error rate, and Type M exaggeration ratio vs. text sample size (n_t), at each term's own empirically-observed effect size, pooled across all six participant sample sizes and 50 replicates/cell."

plot_metrics_vs_x(
  aim1_metrics_by_nt, x_var = "n_t",
  metrics = c("power", "sign_reliability", "type_s_rate", "type_m_ratio"),
  metric_labels = aim1_metric_labels,
  x_lab = "Text sample size (n_t, log scale)"
)
```

This is the one-axis (pooled-over-`n_p`) counterpart of the surface above,
and the visual counterpart of Aim 1's prose finding: `zPCREFp` has the
*worst* sign reliability and the *highest* Type S/Type M values at
`n_t = 2`, worse even than the interaction -- while also having power
*higher* at `n_t = 2` than at `n_t = 10`, the "underpowered paradox"
signature (a significant result here is more likely to be wrong, not more
trustworthy).

##### Mechanism: what the underpowered paradox looks like at the individual-estimate level

The summary diagnostics above (power, sign reliability, Type S/M rates) are
all *aggregates* over 50 replicate fits per cell. It can be easier to see
why the paradox happens by looking at the individual replicate estimates
themselves, rather than only their summary statistics. The three panels
below show every individual estimate from Aim 1's fits at `n_p = 1497` --
the **largest** participant sample size in the grid, held constant across
every row and column so that the funnel shown reflects the text margin
(`n_t`) specifically, not participant-margin noise -- for `zHLVA` (top),
`zPCREFp` (middle), and the `zHLVA:zPCREFp` interaction (bottom): one dot
per replicate fit, one column per simulated true effect size, one row per
text sample size. `zHLVA` is included here (extending the original
two-panel version of this figure) for the same reason the tables/heatmaps
above already treat all three terms symmetrically: since the whole point of
this document is now to compare all three effects on the same footing, not
just the interaction and its text-level counterpart, the mechanism-level
view should do the same. This uses only already-computed replicate
estimates (`results_phase2/aim1_hlva.rds`) -- no new simulation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim1-distribution-explainer
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 12.5
#| fig-cap: "Aim 1: individual estimates (one dot per replicate fit, n_p held constant at its largest grid value, 1497) for zHLVA (top), zPCREFp (middle), and the zHLVA:zPCREFp interaction (bottom), by text sample size (rows, narrower at top) and true effect size (columns, labeled \"true = ...\"). Dashed vertical line = the true value being simulated in that column. Red = a 95% CI that excludes zero (\"significant\"); grey = not significant. A handful of pathological estimates beyond the plotted range (all at n_t = 2) are clipped to the axis edge for readability."

illustrative_n_p <- max(n_p_grid)

make_aim1_distribution_panel <- function(data, term_name, x_clip, illustrative_n_p,
                                          show_x_axis = TRUE) {
  df <- data |>
    dplyr::filter(term == term_name, n_p == illustrative_n_p) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      n_t_f = factor(n_t, levels = n_t_grid),
      significant = ifelse(excludes_zero, "Significant (95% CI excludes 0)", "Not significant"),
      estimate_clipped = pmax(pmin(estimate, x_clip), -x_clip)
    )

  ggplot(df, aes(x = estimate_clipped, y = n_t_f, color = significant, fill = significant)) +
    ggdist::stat_dots(
      side = "both", scale = 0.85, alpha = 0.55,
      binwidth = ggplot2::unit(c(1.3, 2.2), "mm"),
      overflow = "compress"
    ) +
    geom_vline(aes(xintercept = effect_value), linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
    facet_wrap(~effect_value, nrow = 1,
               labeller = as_labeller(function(x) paste0("true = ", x))) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-x_clip, 0, x_clip)) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("Significant (95% CI excludes 0)" = "#b2182b",
                                   "Not significant" = "grey45")) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Significant (95% CI excludes 0)" = "#b2182b",
                                  "Not significant" = "grey45")) +
    labs(
      x = if (show_x_axis) paste0(term_name, " estimate (clipped to [-", x_clip, ", ", x_clip, "])") else NULL,
      y = "n_t", color = NULL, fill = NULL
    ) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      panel.border = element_rect(color = "grey35", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.7),
      panel.spacing = unit(1.1, "lines"),
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey85", color = "grey35"),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8.5),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom"
    )
}

panel_dist_hlva <- make_aim1_distribution_panel(
  aim1_hlva, "zHLVA", x_clip = 2, illustrative_n_p = illustrative_n_p, show_x_axis = FALSE
) + labs(title = "zHLVA (participant-level main effect)")

panel_dist_pcref <- make_aim1_distribution_panel(
  aim1_pcref, "zPCREFp", x_clip = 2, illustrative_n_p = illustrative_n_p, show_x_axis = FALSE
) + labs(title = "zPCREFp (text-level main effect)")

panel_dist_interaction <- make_aim1_distribution_panel(
  aim1_interaction, "zHLVA:zPCREFp", x_clip = 1.5, illustrative_n_p = illustrative_n_p, show_x_axis = TRUE
) + labs(title = "zHLVA:zPCREFp (interaction)")

(panel_dist_hlva / panel_dist_pcref / panel_dist_interaction) +
  patchwork::plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Four things are visible here that the summary tables/plots only imply.
First, the funnel shape itself, present in **all three** rows: each cloud
of dots is wide at the bottom (`n_t = 2`) and collapses to a tight cluster
around the dashed true-value line by the top (`n_t = 136`) -- the textbook
"wide at small *N*, narrow at large *N*" funnel, for every true effect size
simulated, for every term (participant-level or text-level). Second, and
this is the paradox in its most direct form: in `zPCREFp`'s leftmost
column (`true = 0`, i.e. **no true effect at all**), a substantial share of
the `n_t = 2` dots are still colored red -- individually indistinguishable,
in a real analysis, from a genuine discovery. Those red dots at `n_t = 2`
are false positives purely from noise, and they are just as red (just as
"significant", p < .05) as the true positives further right. A
significance threshold cannot tell these apart; only a larger text sample
-- more rows lower down turning into fewer, tighter, more-often-
correctly-colored rows higher up -- can.

Third, `zHLVA`'s top row makes the *contrast* with the text-level terms
directly visible for the first time in this document: its `n_t = 2` funnel
is comparatively narrow already (few dots reach the clip edge), and its
`true = 0` column has only a modest excess of red dots relative to the
nominal 5% -- consistent with its Type I rate staying much closer to
nominal at every `n_t` (Table 2 above). The instability visible in the
`zPCREFp` and interaction rows is not a generic property of "estimating
anything at `n_t = 2`" -- it is specific to terms whose identification
depends on the text margin.

Fourth, comparing the `zPCREFp` and interaction rows directly answers
whether the interaction's funnel looks like `zPCREFp`'s: **not really**. At
`n_t = 2`, the interaction's dots are mostly grey, not red, across every
column including its own empirically-observed effect size (`true = 0.054`)
-- consistent with its much lower power at that cell (0.127, vs.
`zPCREFp`'s 0.627 from the table above). Where `zPCREFp`'s problem at
`n_t = 2` is "too many confidently-wrong answers," the interaction's is
closer to "usually no answer at all, and on the rare occasions there is
one, it is not obviously more trustworthy than `zPCREFp`'s" -- the same
underlying text-margin scarcity, but manifesting as a power problem more
than a false-discovery problem for this particular term.

###### Why can an estimate be "significant" when the true effect is exactly zero?

This is the question the `true = 0` column above raises most sharply, and
it is worth answering mechanistically rather than leaving it as a
statistical curiosity. Two different things are going on, and it is
important to distinguish them.

**It is not simply the ordinary 5% false-positive rate.** A correctly
calibrated 95% CI is *expected* to exclude a true value of zero 5% of the
time, by construction -- that is what "95%" means. But the observed rate at
`n_t = 2` is far above that: the table below shows that 66.3% of the
`zPCREFp` fits at `n_t = 2` under a true null are "significant," roughly
13x the nominal rate. Something is actively miscalibrated here, not merely
unlucky.

**The mechanism is a random-effects identifiability breakdown, not sampling
bad luck on the covariate itself.** With only `n_t = 2` texts, there is
exactly one degree of freedom available to describe how the two sampled
texts differ from each other -- two points determine a line perfectly, with
nothing left over to check whether that line is trustworthy. The "correct"
model asks `glmer` to split any such between-text difference into two
pieces: a text-level random intercept (`(1 | text_id)`, capturing
idiosyncratic, unexplained differences between texts) and the fixed
`zPCREFp` slope (capturing the cohesion effect specifically). Estimating a
random-intercept *variance* from only 2 groups is close to impossible --
there is essentially no information to distinguish "these two texts differ
a lot by chance" from "these two texts differ a lot systematically." In
practice, `lme4` resolves this by pinning the text-level variance at (or
extremely near) its zero boundary -- a **singular fit**:

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim1-singular-fit-diagnostic

null_nt2_diagnostic <- aim1_pcref |>
  dplyr::filter(term == "zPCREFp", n_t == 2, effect_value == 0)

cat("Fit status, all 300 replicates (n_t = 2, true zPCREFp effect = 0):\n")
table(null_nt2_diagnostic$status)

null_nt2_diagnostic |>
  dplyr::group_by(excludes_zero) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n = dplyr::n(),
    `median |estimate|` = round(median(abs(estimate), na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    `median std. error` = round(median(std.error, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Every single one of these 300 replicates converges to a singular fit --
the text-level random-intercept variance collapses to zero every time
`n_t = 2`, regardless of how many participants are simulated. Once that
variance is pinned at zero, the model has nowhere else to put the two
sampled texts' chance difference except into the only fixed-effect
predictor that differs between them -- `zPCREFp`. This inflates the fixed-
effect point estimate (median |estimate| = 0.734 among the "significant"
fits, versus a true value of exactly 0) and simultaneously produces an
overconfident, too-narrow Wald standard error (median SE = 0.106 among the
"significant" fits, versus 0.294 among the fits that correctly stayed
non-significant) -- because the SE formula implicitly assumes the
random-effects variance structure has been reliably estimated, an
assumption that fails precisely at this boundary. Inflated estimate +
deflated SE together push a large share of purely-noise-driven fits across
the 95%-CI-excludes-zero line.

In short: at `n_t = 2`, the model is not really testing "does cohesion
predict comprehension" -- it is testing "do these two specific,
randomly-sampled texts differ," and then attributing 100% of whatever
difference it finds to cohesion, because there is no other place left for
that difference to go. This is a more extreme version of the same
family of problem documented elsewhere in this project as random-effects
misspecification (Aim 3's omitted-`text.id` bias, and Phase 1's finding
that pseudoreplication introduces genuine bias, not just imprecision) --
here the grouping factor is nominally *in* the model formula, but with only
2 groups it is statistically unidentifiable in practice, which behaves much
like omitting it.

#### Visualizations of power and error surfaces: showing power or error rate variation over variation in text sample size x participant sample size, for varying effects

Strictly, **power** is the probability of correctly detecting an effect
that truly exists in the population, under conventional null-hypothesis
significance testing -- it is only a meaningful concept when the true
effect is non-zero. The power surface and the metrics-vs-`n_t` plot above
both hold the true effect size fixed at each term's own observed value;
the figure below instead sweeps the true effect size down to and through
zero for all three terms, so that the same plot shows genuine power curves
(non-zero effect) alongside the **Type I (false-positive) rate** (the
`effect size = 0` case, where there is nothing to detect). Rather than
color that `effect size = 0` line as if it were simply the lightest point
on the same power-curve palette -- which would imply it answers the same
question as its non-zero neighbors -- it is drawn in a distinct,
colorblind-friendly bright orange, held constant across all three rows.

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim1-power-curves
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9.5
#| fig-cap: "Aim 1: classic power curves -- P(significant) vs. participant sample size (n_p, log scale), one row per term, faceted by text sample size (n_t) across columns. Each row uses its own sequential color palette (darker = larger effect size); the thicker line/larger points mark each term's empirically-observed effect size; the bright orange line/points are the Type I (false-positive) rate, i.e. the effect size = 0 case."

aim1_metrics_by_effect <- aim1_sweep_combined |>
  dplyr::group_by(term, effect_value, n_p, n_t) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    power            = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE),
    sign_reliability = mean(correct_sign, na.rm = TRUE),
    coverage         = mean(covers_truth, na.rm = TRUE),
    type_s_rate      = mean(sign_error[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),
    type_m_ratio     = median(inflation_ratio[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Each term sweeps a different set of effect-size values (see the sweep
# grids above), so a single shared color scale across all three rows would
# either compress each term's own 5-point range into indistinguishable
# shades or mix three unrelated numeric scales under one legend. Instead,
# each term gets its own sequential ColorBrewer palette (darker = larger
# effect), and the curve at that term's empirically-observed effect size
# (the middle grid point in every sweep) is drawn thicker and with larger
# points so it is identifiable at a glance. Generalized from the original
# power-only panel builder so the same machinery produces sign-reliability
# and coverage curves below: `metric_var`/`y_lab` select which column to
# plot, `include_zero` drops the true-null point entirely when a metric
# has no meaningful value there (sign reliability -- see prose below), and
# `highlight_zero_orange` controls whether a still-included zero point gets
# the "different question" orange treatment used for power's Type I rate.
make_aim1_curve_panel <- function(term_name, effect_grid, palette_name, metric_var, y_lab,
                                   axis_title = NULL, legend_title = NULL,
                                   include_zero = TRUE, zero_label = "no true effect",
                                   highlight_zero_orange = TRUE, ref_line = NULL, log_y = FALSE,
                                   y_limits = NULL) {
  own_value <- own_effect[[term_name]]
  eff_grid <- if (include_zero) effect_grid else effect_grid[effect_grid != 0]

  # Skip the palette's palest 2 shades (indices 1-2 of the 9-class Brewer
  # palette) before interpolating -- the raw 5-class palette's lightest
  # color is too close to white/background to read easily as a line.
  pal <- grDevices::colorRampPalette(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(9, palette_name)[3:9])(length(eff_grid))
  if (include_zero && highlight_zero_orange && 0 %in% eff_grid) {
    pal[eff_grid == 0] <- "#E69F00"  # Okabe-Ito orange, colorblind-friendly
  }
  effect_labels <- dplyr::case_when(
    eff_grid == 0 & include_zero ~ paste0(eff_grid, " (", zero_label, ")"),
    eff_grid == own_value        ~ paste0(eff_grid, " (observed)"),
    TRUE                         ~ as.character(eff_grid)
  )

  df <- aim1_metrics_by_effect |>
    dplyr::filter(term == term_name, effect_value %in% eff_grid) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      effect_f = factor(effect_value, levels = eff_grid, labels = effect_labels),
      is_own   = effect_value == own_value
    )

  p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = n_p, y = .data[[metric_var]], color = effect_f, group = effect_f)) +
    geom_line(aes(linewidth = is_own)) +
    geom_point(aes(size = is_own)) +
    facet_wrap(~n_t, nrow = 1, labeller = label_both) +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = n_p_grid, labels = scales::label_comma()) +
    scale_color_manual(values = pal, name = legend_title %||% term_name) +
    scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 0.5, `TRUE` = 1.3), guide = "none") +
    scale_size_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 1, `TRUE` = 2.2), guide = "none") +
    labs(x = axis_title, y = y_lab) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 6.5),
      legend.position = "right"
    )

  if (!is.null(ref_line)) {
    p <- p + geom_hline(yintercept = ref_line, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4)
  }
  if (log_y) {
    p <- p + scale_y_log10()
  }
  # coord_cartesian (not scale limits) so a fixed [0, 1] y-axis is shared
  # across power/sign-reliability/coverage/Type S -- directly comparable
  # panel-to-panel -- without silently dropping any data point that might
  # fall (even marginally) outside that range.
  if (!is.null(y_limits)) {
    p <- p + coord_cartesian(ylim = y_limits)
  }
  p
}

panel_hlva <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zHLVA", b_hlva_grid, "Greens",
                                     metric_var = "power", y_lab = "Power",
                                     legend_title = "zHLVA effect size",
                                     zero_label = "no true effect -- Type I rate",
                                     y_limits = c(0, 1))
panel_pcref <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zPCREFp", b_pcref_grid, "Blues",
                                      metric_var = "power", y_lab = "Power",
                                      legend_title = "zPCREFp effect size",
                                      zero_label = "no true effect -- Type I rate",
                                      y_limits = c(0, 1))
panel_interaction <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zHLVA:zPCREFp", b_interaction_grid, "Purples",
                                            metric_var = "power", y_lab = "Power",
                                            axis_title = "Participant sample size (n_p, log scale)",
                                            legend_title = "Interaction effect size",
                                            zero_label = "no true effect -- Type I rate",
                                            y_limits = c(0, 1))

panel_hlva / panel_pcref / panel_interaction
```

The `zPCREFp` row is the most diagnostic: at `n_t = 2`, the bright orange
Type I (false-positive) rate curve (true effect = 0) stays **non-monotonic
and never near zero across the entire `n_p` range** (~20-60%) -- i.e., a
sizeable share of fits at this text sample size are "significant" purely
from noise, regardless of how many participants are added. At larger
`n_t`, that same orange curve flattens out near zero as expected (a
well-calibrated Type I rate), and the colored (genuine power) curves
separate out into a conventional monotonically-rising power curve as `n_p`
grows -- confirming the pathology is specific to the `n_t = 2` regime, not
a general property of `zPCREFp`. This is the clearest single illustration
in this document of the underpowered paradox's mechanism: at the modal
literature text sample size, growing the participant sample does not
rescue the false-positive problem -- it is a text-margin problem, not a
participant-margin one. The highlighted "(observed)" curve in each row --
the effect size actually estimated from this project's real data -- sits in
the middle of its own sweep by construction, letting readers see directly
how much power/error-rate behavior would differ if the true effect were
smaller or larger than what was actually observed.

The same effect-size x `n_p` x `n_t` curve layout can be drawn for **sign
reliability** and **95% CI coverage** as well, using the same
`make_aim1_curve_panel()` machinery as the power curves above -- this
shows whether the same margin-dependence and effect-size sensitivity
apply to those two diagnostics, not just power.

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim1-sign-reliability-curves
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9.5
#| fig-cap: "Aim 1: sign reliability -- P(estimated sign matches true sign) -- vs. participant sample size (n_p, log scale), one row per term, faceted by text sample size (n_t). Layout and color convention match the power curves above, except the true-null (effect = 0) point is omitted (see prose below)."

# Sign reliability has no meaningful value at effect_value = 0: with no
# true effect, sign(true_value) = 0, so `correct_sign` (sign(estimate) ==
# sign(true_value)) is essentially never TRUE by construction, not because
# of any instability -- there is no "correct sign" to recover when there
# is nothing there. The zero point is therefore dropped entirely
# (`include_zero = FALSE`) rather than plotted as a degenerate near-0%
# curve or given the power curves' orange "different question" treatment.
panel_hlva_sr <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zHLVA", b_hlva_grid, "Greens",
                                        metric_var = "sign_reliability", y_lab = "Sign reliability",
                                        legend_title = "zHLVA effect size", include_zero = FALSE,
                                        y_limits = c(0, 1))
panel_pcref_sr <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zPCREFp", b_pcref_grid, "Blues",
                                         metric_var = "sign_reliability", y_lab = "Sign reliability",
                                         legend_title = "zPCREFp effect size", include_zero = FALSE,
                                         y_limits = c(0, 1))
panel_interaction_sr <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zHLVA:zPCREFp", b_interaction_grid, "Purples",
                                               metric_var = "sign_reliability", y_lab = "Sign reliability",
                                               axis_title = "Participant sample size (n_p, log scale)",
                                               legend_title = "Interaction effect size", include_zero = FALSE,
                                               y_limits = c(0, 1))

panel_hlva_sr / panel_pcref_sr / panel_interaction_sr
```

`zPCREFp`'s row again shows the underpowered paradox's flatness signature,
this time on sign reliability rather than power: at `n_t = 2`, sign
reliability sits in the 0.4-0.8 range **across the entire effect-size
sweep**, including its largest simulated effect size (0.35, comparable in
magnitude to `zHLVA`'s own effect) -- and it stays there regardless of
`n_p`, from 25 participants up to the full 1497. Growing the participant
sample at `n_t = 2` does not resolve the coin-flip-adjacent sign
uncertainty even for a comparatively large text-level effect. By contrast,
the same effect size (0.35) reaches ~0.92-1.0 sign reliability once
`n_t = 10`, and a perfect 1.0 by `n_t = 136` at every `n_p`. `zHLVA`'s row
again saturates near 1.0 already at modest `n_p`, independent of `n_t` --
the same participant-margin/text-margin split documented throughout this
section holds for sign reliability just as it does for power.

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim1-coverage-curves
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9.5
#| fig-cap: "Aim 1: 95% CI coverage -- P(the Wald CI contains the true value) -- vs. participant sample size (n_p, log scale), one row per term, faceted by text sample size (n_t). Dotted horizontal line marks nominal 95% coverage. Unlike sign reliability, coverage is well-defined at effect = 0 (a CI can cover a true value of exactly zero) and is included without the orange re-color, since it is not answering a qualitatively different question there -- 95% coverage is the target at every effect size, including zero."

panel_hlva_cov <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zHLVA", b_hlva_grid, "Greens",
                                         metric_var = "coverage", y_lab = "95% CI coverage",
                                         legend_title = "zHLVA effect size",
                                         highlight_zero_orange = FALSE, zero_label = "no true effect",
                                         ref_line = 0.95, y_limits = c(0, 1))
panel_pcref_cov <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zPCREFp", b_pcref_grid, "Blues",
                                          metric_var = "coverage", y_lab = "95% CI coverage",
                                          legend_title = "zPCREFp effect size",
                                          highlight_zero_orange = FALSE, zero_label = "no true effect",
                                          ref_line = 0.95, y_limits = c(0, 1))
panel_interaction_cov <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zHLVA:zPCREFp", b_interaction_grid, "Purples",
                                                metric_var = "coverage", y_lab = "95% CI coverage",
                                                axis_title = "Participant sample size (n_p, log scale)",
                                                legend_title = "Interaction effect size",
                                                highlight_zero_orange = FALSE, zero_label = "no true effect",
                                                ref_line = 0.95, y_limits = c(0, 1))

panel_hlva_cov / panel_pcref_cov / panel_interaction_cov
```

`zPCREFp`'s coverage curves show the clearest and most alarming pattern of
the three metrics covered in this section: at `n_t = 2`, coverage falls
from ~80-86% at `n_p = 25` down to as low as **10-24%** at `n_p` = 1300 or
1497 -- and this collapse happens **at every effect size on the sweep,
including the true-null case** (coverage 0.80 -> 0.16 across the same
`n_p` range when the true effect is exactly zero). That "more data makes
it worse" direction is the opposite of what more participants should do,
and confirms that the overconfident-Wald-SE mechanism documented earlier
in this section (the text-level random-intercept variance collapsing to
zero at `n_t = 2`, in "Why can an estimate be 'significant' when the true
effect is exactly zero?" above) is not a quirk of the one effect size
shown in the earlier error-surfaces figure -- it operates identically
whether or not there is a true effect to detect. `zHLVA` and, to a lesser extent, the interaction
stay much closer to the nominal 95% line (dotted) throughout, again
consistent with their comparative insulation from this project's
chronic text-sample scarcity.

The same treatment extends to the two remaining diagnostics from the
metrics-vs-`n_t` four-panel figure earlier in this section -- **Type S
(sign) error rate** and **Type M (magnitude) ratio** -- both conditional
on significance, so both use the same `include_zero = FALSE` convention
as sign reliability above (a "wrong sign" or "inflation ratio" needs a
true, non-zero sign/magnitude to be wrong or inflated relative to; see the
prose below the figures for the mechanistic detail).

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim1-type-s-curves
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9.5
#| fig-cap: "Aim 1: Type S (sign) error rate -- P(wrong sign | significant) -- vs. participant sample size (n_p, log scale), one row per term, faceted by text sample size (n_t). The true-null (effect = 0) point is omitted, as for sign reliability above: conditioning on significance at a true effect of exactly zero makes Type S trivially ~100% by construction, not informative of miscalibration."

panel_hlva_ts <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zHLVA", b_hlva_grid, "Greens",
                                        metric_var = "type_s_rate", y_lab = "Type S rate",
                                        legend_title = "zHLVA effect size", include_zero = FALSE,
                                        y_limits = c(0, 1))
panel_pcref_ts <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zPCREFp", b_pcref_grid, "Blues",
                                         metric_var = "type_s_rate", y_lab = "Type S rate",
                                         legend_title = "zPCREFp effect size", include_zero = FALSE,
                                         y_limits = c(0, 1))
panel_interaction_ts <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zHLVA:zPCREFp", b_interaction_grid, "Purples",
                                               metric_var = "type_s_rate", y_lab = "Type S rate",
                                               axis_title = "Participant sample size (n_p, log scale)",
                                               legend_title = "Interaction effect size", include_zero = FALSE,
                                               y_limits = c(0, 1))

panel_hlva_ts / panel_pcref_ts / panel_interaction_ts
```

`zPCREFp` again shows the by-now-familiar flat, margin-dependent pattern,
mirroring its own sign-reliability curves (Type S rate is, definitionally,
close to `1 - sign_reliability` among significant fits): at `n_t = 2`,
Type S rates of 30-80% recur across the effect-size sweep regardless of
`n_p` -- a "significant" `zPCREFp` result at this text sample size has a
real chance of pointing the wrong direction even for its largest simulated
effect size. Both main effects' Type S rates fall toward, and mostly reach,
zero by `n_t = 10`-`35`; `zHLVA` is again the most consistently
well-behaved row.

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim1-type-m-curves
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9.5
#| fig-cap: "Aim 1: Type M (magnitude/inflation) ratio -- median |estimate|/|true value| among significant fits -- vs. participant sample size (n_p, log scale), one row per term, faceted by text sample size (n_t). Note the log-scaled y-axis (the ratio spans nearly three orders of magnitude across this grid); the dotted line marks a ratio of 1 (no inflation)."

panel_hlva_tm <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zHLVA", b_hlva_grid, "Greens",
                                        metric_var = "type_m_ratio", y_lab = "Type M ratio (log scale)",
                                        legend_title = "zHLVA effect size", include_zero = FALSE,
                                        ref_line = 1, log_y = TRUE)
panel_pcref_tm <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zPCREFp", b_pcref_grid, "Blues",
                                         metric_var = "type_m_ratio", y_lab = "Type M ratio (log scale)",
                                         legend_title = "zPCREFp effect size", include_zero = FALSE,
                                         ref_line = 1, log_y = TRUE)
panel_interaction_tm <- make_aim1_curve_panel("zHLVA:zPCREFp", b_interaction_grid, "Purples",
                                               metric_var = "type_m_ratio", y_lab = "Type M ratio (log scale)",
                                               axis_title = "Participant sample size (n_p, log scale)",
                                               legend_title = "Interaction effect size", include_zero = FALSE,
                                               ref_line = 1, log_y = TRUE)

panel_hlva_tm / panel_pcref_tm / panel_interaction_tm
```

The log scale is necessary here, not cosmetic: across this grid, the
median Type M ratio among significant fits ranges from ~0.92 (a slight
*under*-estimate, the well-behaved end) up to ~163 at its most extreme
cell -- a span a linear axis could not show without flattening every other
line to the bottom of the plot. As with the error-surfaces figure earlier,
the most extreme ratios cluster at `n_t = 2` for the smallest simulated
non-zero effect sizes (where a small absolute bias divided by an even
smaller true value inflates dramatically) -- and the same interpretive
caveat applies: a large Type M ratio at a small true effect size reflects
that effect size's small denominator as much as it reflects the estimate's
absolute error. `zPCREFp`'s row still stands out among the two main-effect
terms, with ratios remaining elevated (typically 1.5-10x, worse at smaller
`n_p`) at `n_t = 2` even for its larger simulated effect sizes (0.2, 0.35).
`zHLVA` settles close to the dotted no-inflation line by `n_t = 35` at
every `n_p` and every non-zero effect size; the interaction does too for
its own empirically-observed effect size (0.054) and larger, though its
*smallest* simulated effect size (0.025) still shows non-trivial inflation
at `n_t = 35` when `n_p` is also small (ratio ~4-8x at `n_p` = 25-100) --
consistent with the general point above that Type M ratios are most
exaggerated, and least representative of a "typical" absolute error, when
the true effect being divided by is itself very small.

## Aim 2: discovery/replication rates

| `n_t` | zHLVA replication | zPCREFp replication | interaction replication |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0.478 | 0.473 | **0.013** |
| 10 | 0.803 | 0.157 | 0.250 |
| 35 | 0.797 | 0.163 | 0.267 |
| 85 | 0.820 | 0.237 | 0.273 |
| 136 | 0.797 | 0.340 | 0.297 |

A different, complementary picture emerges here: under the stricter
"significant in both independent halves, same sign" criterion, the
**interaction is the most fragile of the three** at `n_t = 2` (1.3%
replication vs. ~47-48% for both main effects) -- because it is so rarely
even significant in the first place with half the already-small sample. So:
Aim 1's sign-reliability diagnostic (conditional on significance) points to
`zPCREFp` as the least trustworthy; Aim 2's replication-rate diagnostic
(unconditional, halved samples) points to the interaction as the most
fragile overall. Both are real, non-contradictory findings -- they answer
different practical questions ("if I got a significant result, can I trust
its sign?" vs. "if I ran this again, would I get the same answer?") -- and
both indicate `n_t = 2` is inadequate, just via different mechanisms.

The table below defines Aim 2's three discovery/replication diagnostics and
states exactly how each is computed. All three are derived from
`combine_replication_p2()`'s per-cell pairing of two independently-fit
halves (`discovery` and `replication`, each `n_p_total`/`n_t_total` split
roughly in half by `generate_data_p2_pair()`), using the same Wald-CI
`excludes_zero` significance criterion as Aim 1, then aggregated by
`term` x `n_t` (pooled over `n_p` and the 50 replicate pairs/cell).

| Diagnostic | Standard definition | Computed here as |
|---|---|---|
| `discovery_rate` | P(significant in an initial/"discovery" sample) -- how often a first look at data of this size turns up a significant result at all, regardless of whether it is subsequently confirmed. | `mean(discovery_significant)`, where `discovery_significant = excludes_zero` evaluated on the **discovery** half alone. |
| `replication_rate` | Unconditional replication rate: P(significant **and** same-signed in *both* independent halves) -- Marek et al.'s (2022) Fig. 3e-style replication probability. | `mean(replicated)`, where `replicated = excludes_zero_discovery & excludes_zero_replication & sign(estimate_discovery) == sign(estimate_replication)`. Both halves must independently clear the significance threshold *and* agree in sign. |
| `conditional_replication` | Conditional replication rate: P(replicates \| already significant in the discovery half) -- "given I got a significant result once, would it hold up in an independent second sample?" | `mean(replicated[discovery_significant])`, i.e. `replicated` restricted to rows where the discovery half was already significant. More decision-relevant than the unconditional rate for a researcher who has already observed one significant result, since it factors out the "was it significant even once" question that `discovery_rate` alone answers. |

Note the arithmetic relationship between all three: `replication_rate` is
mechanically bounded above by `discovery_rate` (a discovery is a
prerequisite for replication), and `conditional_replication =
replication_rate / discovery_rate` for any cell where `discovery_rate > 0`
-- so a low unconditional `replication_rate` can reflect either a low
`discovery_rate` (rarely significant even once, a power problem) or a low
`conditional_replication` (often significant once but rarely again, a
genuine replication-failure problem), and distinguishing these two
mechanisms is exactly why all three are reported rather than
`replication_rate` alone (see the discussion of the interaction's `n_t = 2`
numbers below).

### Aim 2 -- fuller metrics table and visualizations

In addition to the raw replication rate above, the table and figure below
add the discovery rate and conditional replication rate defined above.

```{r}
#| label: aim2-full-metrics-table

aim2_metrics_by_nt <- aim2_all |>
  dplyr::group_by(term, n_t) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    discovery_rate           = mean(discovery_significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    replication_rate         = mean(replicated, na.rm = TRUE),
    conditional_replication  = mean(replicated[discovery_significant], na.rm = TRUE),
    n_fits                   = dplyr::n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

aim2_metrics_by_nt |>
  dplyr::arrange(term, n_t) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Term", "n_t", "Discovery rate", "Replication rate",
                  "Conditional replication", "n fits")
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim2-metrics-vs-nt
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-cap: "Aim 2: discovery rate, (unconditional) replication rate, and conditional replication rate vs. text sample size, at each term's own empirically-observed effect size."

plot_metrics_vs_x(
  aim2_metrics_by_nt, x_var = "n_t",
  metrics = c("discovery_rate", "replication_rate", "conditional_replication"),
  metric_labels = aim2_metric_labels,
  x_lab = "Text sample size (n_t, log scale)"
)
```

The third panel adds a finding not visible in the unconditional
replication-rate table alone: conditional on having found a significant
interaction in the discovery half, the interaction's replication rate (~22%
at `n_t = 2`, rising to ~70-92% at larger `n_t`) is *lower* than `zHLVA`'s at
every `n_t` but is **not as catastrophically low** as its unconditional
replication rate (1.3% at `n_t = 2`) might suggest in isolation -- most of
that unconditional fragility comes from rarely being significant in the
discovery half at all (a power problem), rather than from significant
discoveries failing to hold up (a pure replication problem). Both framings
matter for different audiences: a reviewer asking "is this literature's
replication rate adequate" should look at the unconditional rate; a
researcher who has already observed one significant result and is deciding
whether to trust it should look at the conditional rate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-aim2-replication-surface
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Aim 2: unconditional replication-rate surface across the full joint (n_p, n_t) grid, at each term's own empirically-observed effect size -- the discovery/replication analog of the Aim 1 power surface above."

aim2_surface <- aim2_all |>
  dplyr::group_by(term, n_p, n_t) |>
  dplyr::summarise(replication_rate = mean(replicated, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

plot_power_heatmap(aim2_surface, fill_var = "replication_rate", fill_label = "Replication\nrate")
```

Similar to Aim 1's power surface, but stricter, and carrying the same
`zPCREFp`-specific caveat identified there (numbers checked directly
against `aim2_surface`). `zHLVA` saturates cleanly on the participant
margin alone once `n_t >= 10` (100% replication by `n_p = 375`), but at
`n_t = 2` its replication rate lags well behind -- 54-80% across `n_p =
375`-1497, never reaching 100% anywhere on this grid -- so halving the
sample still measurably hurts even the best-behaved term when `n_t = 2`.
The **interaction** shows the pattern the paragraph above expected:
replication stays under 5% at every `n_p` when `n_t = 2`, then climbs to
48-68% once `n_t >= 10` and `n_p >= 1300`, topping out at 68% (`n_p =
1497`, `n_t = 85` or `136`) -- a real gain from more texts. **`zPCREFp`
again breaks that expectation**, just as it did for power: its two
highest replication rates on the entire grid (0.78 and 0.80) both occur
at `n_t = 2` (`n_p = 1300` and `1497` respectively) -- higher than
anything it achieves at any larger `n_t`, including the largest-both-
margins cell (0.64 at `n_p = 1497, n_t = 136`). This is the same
underpowered-paradox signature carrying over from Aim 1's power surface
into Aim 2's stricter replication criterion, not a genuine advantage of
the smallest text sample.

## Aim 1 & Aim 2: discussion

Comparing the two aims' diagnostics side by side clarifies what each is, and
isn't, telling us:

- **Aim 1** (conditional on significance) says `zPCREFp` is the *least*
  trustworthy term at `n_t = 2` -- its significant results are the most
  likely to have the wrong sign.
- **Aim 2** (unconditional, halved samples) says the **interaction** is the
  most fragile overall -- not because its significant results are
  especially untrustworthy, but because it is rarely significant at all
  once the sample is halved.
- Both agree that `n_t = 2` -- the modal text sample size in this project's
  literature review (Phase 1's overlay finding: ~95% of reviewed studies
  fall outside the trustworthy region) -- is inadequate for any of the
  three effects, via different mechanisms depending on which question is
  asked.
- `zHLVA`, the sole participant-level effect among the three, is
  comparatively well-behaved on both diagnostics and saturates on the
  participant margin alone, independent of text sample size -- consistent
  with Phase 1's finding that participant-margin effects are far less
  sensitive to this project's chronic text-sample scarcity than text-margin
  effects are. This is now visible on every diagnostic in this document
  (the fuller metrics table's explicit Type I column, the reordered power
  surface/curves, and the three-panel funnel plot), not just the original
  sign-reliability/power comparison -- the general pattern (text-margin
  terms behave qualitatively differently from the participant-margin term,
  regardless of which specific error-taxonomy diagnostic is examined) holds
  up consistently, which is itself the more general finding this
  restructured document is built to surface.

A full cross-aim synthesis, tying these findings together with Aims 3-6
(random-effects misspecification, variance-component sensitivity, slope/
covariance recovery, and design remedies), will appear once those aims have
their own reporting-ready documents.

## Flagged future work

- **The significance-threshold/multiple-comparisons sweep** (Marek et al.'s
  P<0.05-to-Bonferroni comparison) was explicitly deferred at the design
  stage, given the real core model's 26-term fixed-effects formula. Aim 1/2
  above use a single 95%-CI-based threshold throughout; whether Aim 1's
  error-rate findings hold up under a stricter multiple-comparisons
  correction remains untested.
- **Extension decisions** (recorded after discussion with the user; none
  implemented in this pass -- see `cost-estimate-expanded-grid-replicates-aims1-2-PLAN.qmd`
  for the full cost-estimation method and all six candidate scenarios; the
  ones referenced by the decisions below are summarized here so this
  document is self-contained). All scenarios assume the same 4-worker
  `furrr` setup and 3 sweeps x 5 effect values x 3 fits/replicate as the
  current run; scale factor and wall-clock are relative to/estimated from
  the achieved 67,500-fit, ~5h baseline (Scenario 0):

All seven scenarios from the source document are listed below, for
completeness. Scenarios 1-3 (greyed out) are not referenced by name in
the decisions that follow -- they sit between Scenario 0 and Scenario 4 in
both cost and scope, and were superseded by the bundled Scenario 4+5
decision below rather than chosen individually.

  | Scenario | Change | Total fits | Scale factor | Est. wall-clock (4 workers) |

  1. **Densify both margins of the `n_p`/`n_t` grid** (Scenario 4, ~3.3x
     cost) **and increase replicates from 50 to 100 in the same run**
     (bundled with densification per the user's preference, rather than as
     a separate job) -- together, this is Scenario 5 in the cost-estimate
     document: ~445,500 fits, ~33h wall-clock on 4 workers, ~132
     core-hours. This becomes the next full-grid run superseding the
     current 30-cell/50-replicate results once launched.
  2. **Extending the sample-size range beyond this project's real N**
     (Scenario 6 above; e.g. `n_p` = 3000/5000, `n_t` = 200/300) is not
     ruled out, and the benchmark the user asked for (a handful of single
     fits at candidate large `n_p`/`n_t` values) has now been run --
     summarized below -- resolving the "not reliably extrapolable"
