## Scenario 6 benchmark (completed)

6 candidate cells at the proposed extremes (`n_p` up to 5000, `n_t` up to
300), 2 replicates each, `"correct"` RE spec, timed with the same
`generate_data_p2()`/`fit_model_p2()` helpers used throughout this
document (full detail and the underlying findings are in
`cost-estimate-expanded-grid-replicates-aims1-2-PLAN.qmd`'s "Scenario 6
benchmark" section):

| Cell | `n_p` | `n_t` | Rows | Mean fit time | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Text-margin only | 1497 | 200 | 59,880 | 2.93s | clean, both reps |
| Text-margin only | 1497 | 300 | 59,880 | 3.50s | clean, both reps |
| Participant-margin only | 3000 | 136 | 120,000 | 7.18s | clean, both reps |
| Participant-margin only | 5000 | 136 | 200,000 | 12.18s | clean, both reps |
| Both margins | 3000 | 300 | 120,000 | 7.65s | clean, both reps |
| Both margins (max) | 5000 | 300 | 200,000 | 11.68s | clean, both reps |

All 12 fits converged cleanly (no singular fits, optimizer warnings, or
timeouts). Fit time normalizes to **0.049-0.064 sec per 1,000 rows**
(mean 0.058) across every cell -- matching the existing baseline's implied
rate (0.059 sec/1,000 rows) almost exactly, with no evidence that fitting
gets disproportionately harder at very large `n_p`/`n_t`. A second,
practically useful finding: because `generate_data_p2()` caps each
participant at `k = min(10, n_texts)` assigned texts, extending `n_t`
*alone* past 10 adds no rows and costs essentially nothing extra (the
`n_t = 200`/`300` cells cost the same as the existing `n_t = 136`
baseline at matched `n_p`) -- only extending `n_p`, or adding more
texts-per-participant, increases cost.

As one concrete illustration: a dedicated sweep restricted to just these 6
cells, at the existing Aims 1-2 structure (3 sweeps x 5 effect values x 50
replicates/cell), would cost ~9.4h serial / ~2.4h on 4 workers (Aim 1
only, 4,500 fits) or ~28.2h serial / ~7.0h on 4 workers (full Aim 1 + Aim
2 structure, 13,500 fits, upper-bound estimate). A full densified-and-
extended Scenario 6 grid (the original "~130-150 cells" estimate) can now
be costed with the same confidence as Scenarios 1-4 via `rows x 0.06 /
1000` seconds per fit, once a specific grid is chosen.
:::
  3. **A dedicated `b_intercept` sweep** was judged worth scoping as its
     own small follow-up study to check whether logistic regression's
     non-collapsibility makes the text-margin instability findings above
     sensitive to this project's unusually high (~89%) baseline accuracy.
     It has since been designed and costed in full (see
     `cost-estimate-b-intercept-sweep-PLAN.qmd`), summarized here:

     ::: {.callout-note}
     ## `b_intercept` sweep design and cost (run)

     A 5-point one-at-a-time sweep over target baseline accuracies (0.50,
     0.65, 0.80, **0.89 -- observed**, 0.95, i.e. `b_intercept` = 0, 0.619,
     1.386, 2.093, 2.944), holding the three focal effect sizes at their
     empirically-observed values, at **4 representative cells** rather
     than the full 30-cell grid: the existing small (25, 2), moderate
     (375, 35), and large (1497, 136) benchmark cells, plus a new
     `n_t = 2` pathology cell at large `n_p` (1497, 2) -- benchmarked
     specifically for this plan at 0.78s/fit (mean of 2 reps, both
     `converged_singular`) -- chosen to isolate whether the text-margin
     identifiability breakdown itself is intercept-sensitive. Aim 1
     diagnostics only (no discovery/replication split), 50 replicates/
     cell: **1,000 total fits, ~22 minutes serial, ~5.6 minutes
     wall-clock on 4 workers** -- cheap enough to run interactively, no
     background job needed. A design check run as part of this planning
     pass found the simulated data's actual mean response rate runs
     1-2 percentage points below the naive `plogis(b_intercept)` target
     at every grid point (expected, from the same non-collapsibility/
     Jensen's-inequality logic this sweep investigates) -- the achieved,
     not nominal, baseline should be reported in any write-up.
     :::

     The sweep was subsequently run in full; see "`b_intercept` sweep:
     results" below (its own top-level section, placed after this list,
     since its code chunk did not nest cleanly inside this indented
     callout/list structure).
- **The shareable self-contained workflow** (a standalone `.R` process
  script + bash runner, updated generation/visualization tutorials sourcing
  from it, and a final trimmed reporting document) is planned as a
  follow-on piece of work once the extension decisions above are settled,
  so that any new grid only needs to be run once against the final
  pipeline.

Aims 3-6's own flagged-future-work items (Aim 3's `brms` spot-checks, Aim
4's flat interaction-CI-width finding, Aim 5's deferred joint
correlation x variance sweep, Aim 6's remedy-specific follow-ups, and the
`furrr` load-imbalance engineering note) are unchanged and documented in
`phase2-effect-variance-misspecification.qmd`; they will surface again in
their own future documents rather than being duplicated here.

## `b_intercept` sweep: results

The sweep designed and costed above (design summary: "`b_intercept`
sweep design and cost" callout in "Flagged future work") was run (script:
`run_b_intercept_sweep.R`) -- **sequentially rather than with `furrr`'s 4
workers**, given the real memory pressure this machine was found to be
under when this sweep was designed (swap ~87% full at the time); actual
runtime was **20.7 minutes** (vs. the ~5.6-minute parallel estimate),
still cheap enough to run interactively. Results are saved to
`results_phase2/aim1_intercept_sweep.rds` (1,000 fits x 3 terms = 3,000
rows) and loaded directly below, not recomputed.

See `cost-estimate-b-intercept-sweep-PLAN.qmd` for the fuller design,
execution, and results write-up (including the same findings below in
more detail, a projected-vs-achieved cost comparison, and the follow-on
"Scenario 5 + intercept variation" work this sweep's findings motivated).

```{r}
#| label: fig-b-intercept-sweep-results
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "b_intercept sweep: power vs. target baseline accuracy, by representative cell and term. Vertical dotted line marks this project's real, observed baseline (~89%)."

intercept_sweep_results <- readRDS("results_phase2/aim1_intercept_sweep.rds")

intercept_sweep_summary <- intercept_sweep_results |>
  dplyr::group_by(label, n_p, n_t, target_accuracy, term) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    power            = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE),
    sign_reliability = mean(correct_sign, na.rm = TRUE),
    type_s_rate      = mean(sign_error[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),
    type_m_ratio     = median(inflation_ratio[excludes_zero], na.rm = TRUE),
    coverage         = mean(covers_truth, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell_label = paste0(label, " (n_p=", n_p, ", n_t=", n_t, ")"))

ggplot(intercept_sweep_summary, aes(x = target_accuracy, y = power, color = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.890, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~cell_label, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Target baseline accuracy (plogis(b_intercept))", y = "Power", color = "Term") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Headline finding: power for all three effects generally declines as
baseline accuracy rises toward this project's real ~89% value**, most
clearly for the interaction and `zPCREFp` -- confirming the concern that
motivated this sweep. At the "moderate" cell (n_p=375, n_t=35), the
interaction's power declines close to monotonically from 84% (50%
accuracy) to 28% (95% accuracy); at the "small" cell (n_p=25, n_t=2),
`zHLVA`'s power declines from 32% to 6% over the same range. The `n_t =
2` pathology cell's Type S rate for `zPCREFp` also *worsens* toward
higher accuracy (36% -> 55% wrong-sign-given-significant), as does its
Type M ratio (4.2x -> 7.5x) -- so the text-margin identifiability
breakdown documented throughout the main part of this document is not
merely co-occurring with this project's high baseline accuracy, it is
measurably *exacerbated* by it.

**A specific mechanistic finding, investigated directly**: at the
"large" cell (n_p=1497, n_t=136), the interaction's power looks like it
drops suddenly -- a flat 100% from 50-89% accuracy, then a step down to
78% only at the most extreme point (95%) -- which could look like a
discontinuity or an artifact. Inspecting the underlying per-replicate
`estimate/std.error` ratios shows this is not a sudden change in the
data-generating mechanism: the median ratio declines smoothly and
continuously across the *entire* sweep (5.70 -> 5.58 -> 4.92 -> 3.73 ->
2.86), and so does the minimum (3.26 -> 3.25 -> 2.53 -> 2.05 -> 1.17).
What changes abruptly is only whether that smooth decline crosses the
fixed 95%-significance threshold (a ratio of 1.96): because the starting
margin at 50% accuracy is generous (median ratio ~5.7, nearly 3x the
threshold), it takes until the most extreme grid point for enough
replicates' ratios to dip below 1.96 (11 of 50 do, at 95% accuracy; zero
do at every lower level, including 89%, where the *minimum* ratio was
already down to 2.05 -- a near miss). This is a textbook case of a
smoothly-varying quantity producing an apparently sudden change in a
*thresholded* summary (power) -- compounded by a genuine, accelerating
increase in standard error as the baseline approaches the ceiling: mean
SE rises from 0.0095 to 0.0174 across the sweep, and the *rate* of
increase itself accelerates (successive ratios 1.02x, 1.14x, 1.22x,
1.30x), loosely tracking the Fisher-information-style prediction that
variance in a Bernoulli outcome scales with `1/(p(1-p))` (a naive
`1/sqrt(p(1-p))` calculation predicts a 2.29x relative SE increase from
50% to 95% accuracy; the observed increase, 1.83x, is smaller, plausibly
buffered by the participant/text random-effects variance components, but
points the same direction). This prediction -- that a denser grid near
the top of the accuracy range would reveal a smooth decline rather than
a true discontinuity at exactly 95% -- was tested directly (see
"Follow-up: ceiling-densification check" immediately below) and
confirmed.

### Follow-up: ceiling-densification check (confirmed)

Two more intercept values, 92% and 97% target accuracy, were added at
the same 4 cells and 50 replicates/cell (script:
`run_b_intercept_sweep_ceiling_extension.R`; 400 additional fits, 8.7
minutes serial), specifically to test the smooth-decline prediction
above. Results are saved separately
(`results_phase2/aim1_intercept_sweep_ceiling_extension.rds`) and
combined with the original sweep below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b-intercept-ceiling-extension
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "b_intercept sweep with ceiling densification: power vs. target baseline accuracy, by representative cell and term, now at 7 accuracy points (adding 92% and 97% to the original 5). Vertical dotted line marks this project's real, observed baseline (~89%)."

intercept_sweep_ceiling_ext <- readRDS("results_phase2/aim1_intercept_sweep_ceiling_extension.rds")

intercept_sweep_combined <- dplyr::bind_rows(intercept_sweep_results, intercept_sweep_ceiling_ext)

intercept_sweep_combined_summary <- intercept_sweep_combined |>
  dplyr::group_by(label, n_p, n_t, target_accuracy, term) |>
  dplyr::summarise(power = mean(excludes_zero, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell_label = paste0(label, " (n_p=", n_p, ", n_t=", n_t, ")"))

ggplot(intercept_sweep_combined_summary, aes(x = target_accuracy, y = power, color = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.890, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~cell_label, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(x = "Target baseline accuracy (plogis(b_intercept))", y = "Power", color = "Term") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Confirmed**: at the "large" cell, the interaction's power across all 7
points is 100%, 100%, 100%, 100%, **92%, 78%, 68%** (50%/65%/80%/89%/
**92%/95%/97%** accuracy) -- a smooth, monotonic decline once the two
new points fill in the gap, not a discontinuity at exactly 95%. The
underlying `estimate/std.error` ratios decline just as smoothly across
all 7 points (median: 5.70, 5.58, 4.92, 3.73, **3.31, 2.86, 2.32**;
minimum: 3.26, 3.25, 2.53, 2.05, **1.31, 1.17, 0.297**), and mean SE
keeps rising with the same accelerating pattern (0.0095, 0.0097, 0.0110,
0.0134, **0.0146, 0.0174, 0.0221**). The same pattern generalizes beyond
the one cell originally flagged: the "moderate" cell's interaction power
also continues declining smoothly past the original grid's endpoint,
from 48% (89%) down to 36%, 28%, and 22% at 92%/95%/97% accuracy. The
apparent "cliff" in the original 5-point grid was, as predicted, a grid-
sparsity artifact rather than a true discontinuity -- confirming that
this project's underpowered-paradox-adjacent findings do not depend on a
sudden qualitative change happening to fall near the observed baseline;
the underlying erosion is continuous and only *looks* abrupt because of
where the significance threshold happens to sit relative to a sparse
grid.

**Interpretation**: this project's own real baseline accuracy (~89%)
sits close enough to the region where these effects begin measurably
eroding that the main Aims 1-2 document's findings should be read as
somewhat conservative, not baseline-independent -- a comprehension test
with a more moderate pass rate would likely show *better* power and
*less* severe Type S/M error for the same underlying effect sizes, not
worse.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Development history (collapsed -- process detail, not reportable findings)

This section preserves the process/decision narrative that accompanied the
original build of Aims 1-2, condensed from `phase2-effect-variance-misspecification-PLAN.qmd`
and `phase2-effect-variance-misspecification.qmd`. Nothing in this section
is required to understand the results above; it documents how they were
produced.

### Relationship to existing project simulation infrastructure

This work explicitly reused conventions already established in
`simulation_study_complete.qmd` (Simulations 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6) and
`power-simulation-vocabulary-cohesion.qmd`, rather than inventing new ones:

- **One-at-a-time sweeps, not a full factorial.** Existing simulations vary
  one dimension (effect size, a single variance component, or a single
  intercept-slope correlation) at a time while holding others fixed at a
  realistic value, to avoid combinatorial explosion. Phase 2 follows the
  same pattern (six aims, altogether) rather than crossing effect size x
  variance x covariance x misspecification x design strategy x
  two-dimensional sample size all at once.
- **Fitting**: `glmer` (fast) as the sweep workhorse, with `brms`
  spot-checks at a handful of cells using the project's precompile-once,
  `update()`-per-replicate pattern to avoid Stan recompilation cost across
  replicates (not run for Aims 1-2 specifically; see flagged future work).
- **Parallelization**: `furrr::future_pmap_dfr()` with `multisession`,
  `furrr_options(seed = TRUE)`, hierarchical seeds, 4 workers with a
  `setTimeLimit()` guard, following Phase 1's memory-safety lessons.
- **Outcome-quality classification**: converged-clean / converged-singular
  / optimizer-warning / error, reused verbatim from Phase 1's helper
  functions.

### Confirmed decisions (made before building Aims 1-2)

1. **Scope**: all six aims cover **three effects** -- `zHLVA` (main),
   `zPCREFp` (main), and `zHLVA:zPCREFp` (interaction) -- rather than the
   interaction alone.
2. **Aim 2 split axis**: left configurable (`split_margin =
   "participants_only"` vs. `"both"`) rather than fixed; both variants can
   be run and compared. The results above use `"participants_only"`.
3. **Significance-threshold sweep**: deferred (see "Flagged future work").
4. **Pacing**: build and review Aim 1 (together with Aim 2) first, as the
   more traditional power-analysis-style starting point extended with the
   replication-split question.
5. **Replicate count**: 50 resamples/cell, matching Phase 1 Step 3's
   memory-safe, coarsened configuration.

### Timing benchmark

A small number of representative cells (small/moderate/large) were timed
once each for the `"correct"` and `"misspecified"` RE specifications (the
two used by Aims 1-3), before committing to the full grid:

| Cell | n_p | n_t | `correct` | `misspecified` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| small | 25 | 2 | 0.34s (singular) | 0.03s (clean) |
| moderate | 375 | 35 | 0.71s (clean) | 0.30s (clean) |
| large | 1497 | 136 | 3.53s (clean) | 1.43s (clean) |

Mean per-fit time across these three cells (a rough, order-of-magnitude
estimate, not a proper average over the full grid's cell-size
distribution): `correct` ~1.53s, `misspecified` ~0.59s. (The original
benchmark also timed a `"full_slopes"` arm for Aim 5's covariance sweep,
using reference slope-variance/correlation values extracted from the fitted
core model; that arm is out of scope for this Aims-1/2-only document and is
reported instead in the Aim 5 document.)

Extrapolated cost: Aim 1 (22,500 fits, `correct` spec) ~9.6h serial / ~2.4h
on 4 workers; Aim 2 (~22,500 fits, `correct` spec) ~9.6h serial / ~2.4h
parallel. Combined, each `(sweep, effect_value, n_p, n_t, rep)` combination
triggers **three** `glmer` fits (one Aim 1 full-sample fit, plus Aim 2's
discovery and replication half-sample fits): 3 sweeps x 5 effect values x 30
cells x 50 reps = 22,500 combinations x 3 fits = **67,500 total fits**,
estimated at ~20h serial / ~5h on 4 parallel workers.

### Validation: small-scale smoke test

Before committing to the full grid, the pipeline was validated on a 24-cell
subset (2 effect values x 2 participant Ns x 2 text Ns x 3 reps, interaction
sweep only, at small sample sizes). Kept live here (cheap, ~6 seconds) as a
lightweight regression check that `generate_data_p2()`/`fit_model_p2()`
above still behave as expected.

```{r}
#| label: aim1-aim2-smoke-test
#| cache: true

smoke_grid <- tidyr::crossing(
  sweep = "interaction",
  effect_value = c(0, 0.054),
  n_p = c(25, 100),
  n_t = c(2, 10),
  rep = 1:3
)

smoke_results <- purrr::pmap(smoke_grid, run_aim1_aim2_cell)
aim1_smoke <- purrr::map_dfr(smoke_results, "aim1")
aim2_smoke <- purrr::map_dfr(smoke_results, "aim2")
```

```{r}
#| label: aim1-aim2-smoke-test-check

aim1_smoke |> dplyr::filter(term == "zHLVA:zPCREFp") |>
  dplyr::select(n_p, n_t, effect_value, rep, estimate, ci_lower, ci_upper,
                excludes_zero, correct_sign, status)

aim2_smoke |> dplyr::filter(term == "zHLVA:zPCREFp") |>
  dplyr::select(n_p, n_t, effect_value, rep, discovery_significant, replicated,
                status_discovery, status_replication)
```

The pipeline ran the 24-cell subset in ~5.6 seconds and produced sensible,
correctly-structured output for both Aim 1 (per-term bias/CI/sign
diagnostics) and Aim 2 (discovery/replication agreement) -- singular fits
were common at these smallest cells (`n_p = 25`, `n_t = 2`), as expected.

### Cost note and launch record

The full grid was not run interactively. It was launched as a detached
background process (`run_aim1_aim2_full.R`), one sweep at a time (`hlva`,
`pcref`, `interaction`), using `furrr::plan(multisession, workers = 4)`. All
three sweeps finished in ~99-101 minutes each (~5h total on 4 parallel
workers, matching the benchmark-derived estimate closely). Results were
saved to `results_phase2/aim{1,2}_{sweep}.rds` and are what this document
loads above.
:::

## Follow-up note

The DGP and fitting code above (`generate_data_p2()`, `fit_model_p2()`,
`generate_data_p2_pair()`, `run_aim1_aim2_cell()`) is kept live in this
document, unmodified from the version used to produce the saved results, so
it can be inspected and -- in a future, separate turn -- modified if
specific changes turn out to be informative. No new simulation runs have
been made in this pass; any modification to this code that would justify a
new full-grid run (a multi-hour, background-job undertaking) should be
discussed and scoped before being launched.
